questions.question: Explain why a partnership keeps a fixed capital account AND a current account for each partner, and state what the agreement of Molefe and de Waal promises each partner before profits are shared.
questions.expected_answer: The capital account records each partner's permanent investment — Molefe R400 000 and de Waal R300 000 — and stays fixed, moving only on a formal contribution or withdrawal. This keeps the base for interest on capital and the profit-sharing ratio stable, and shows readers the partners' long-term commitment. The current account records everything that flows between partner and business during the year: interest on capital, salary, bonus and profit share credited; drawings debited. A credit balance means the business owes the partner; a debit balance means the partner has drawn ahead of earnings. The agreement promises interest on capital at 9 percent — R36 000 to Molefe and R27 000 to de Waal — salaries of R120 000 to Molefe and R144 000 to de Waal, a R10 000 bonus to de Waal if the sales target is met, and the remaining profit shared four to three, the ratio of their capitals.

questions.question: Give the double entries for the two adjustments new to grade 11 — creating and later adjusting the provision for bad debts, and capitalising interest on the loan — and trace the loan balance through the year.
questions.expected_answer: Creating the provision: debtors are R48 000 and 5 percent is provided, so debit Provision for bad debts adjustment R2 400 and credit Provision for bad debts R2 400; debtors are then shown at R45 600. The next year the provision is adjusted, not recreated: debtors of R56 000 need a provision of R2 800, so debit Provision for bad debts adjustment R400 and credit Provision for bad debts R400 — only the movement touches profit; a decrease would be credited to the adjustment account as income. Capitalised interest: debit Interest on loan R18 000 and credit Loan R18 000, because the bank adds the interest to the debt and no money moves. The loan balance: opening R150 000 plus capitalised interest R18 000 gives R168 000, less the repayment of R30 000, closing at R138 000 — opening plus interest less repayments equals closing.

questions.question: Explain which year-end adjustments are reversed on 1 March, which are not, and why the reversal prevents the February telephone account of R1 850 from being counted twice.
questions.expected_answer: The four timing adjustments are reversed exactly: accrued expenses, prepaid expenses, income received in advance and accrued income — each moved an amount across the year-end boundary, so each is flipped on the first day of the new year. Depreciation, trading stock deficit, bad debts and the provision for bad debts are never reversed, because they record value permanently consumed or lost, not a shuffle between years. For the telephone: at year end we debited Telephone and credited Accrued expenses with R1 850. On 1 March the reversal debits Accrued expenses and credits Telephone, so the telephone account opens the new year with a credit of R1 850. When the bill arrives and the payment of R1 850 is posted as a debit, the account nets to nil for that bill — the expense is counted once, in the year it belongs to, satisfying the matching principle by structure rather than by the bookkeeper's memory.
